title: Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde — Episode 4
subtitle: The end of Robert Louis Stevenson's novella: a visitor at midnight, a glass that changes colour, and a respectable man's full confession.
crosslink: Need an easier version? Read this episode at A2/B1 level →  ·  ← Episode 3
intention: you'll read the two documents that explain everything, and use the grammar of regret — If I had never…, I would not now…; I wish I hadn't…; If only… — to judge a man who could have stopped at any moment, and didn't.
previously: Jekyll shut himself away, and Dr Lanyon, after one terrible shock, refused to speak his name and died within weeks, leaving Utterson a sealed envelope “not to be opened till the death or disappearance of Dr. Henry Jekyll”. Then Poole came for Utterson: for a week the voice in the cabinet had not been his master's, and it had been sending him to every chemist in London for a drug. They broke down the door and found Hyde dead, in clothes far too large for him — and no trace of Jekyll. On the desk: a new will in Utterson's favour, a note, and a sealed confession.
warmup: Last time you predicted what the two documents would reveal. Were you right?
Most people behave slightly differently at work, with family and with old friends. Are they different people — or one person with different sides?
If you could take a drink that let you do anything for one night with no one ever knowing it was you, would you take it? Be honest.
vocab_intro: Ten words for the final episode. Think first — the Reveal only confirms.

vocab.heading: A · What do they mean here? Work it out from the sentence
vocab.instruction: Read each sentence aloud and say what the bold word means from the rest of the sentence. Then reveal.

items.sent: The politician gave speeches about honesty in public, while in private he took money from both sides. For years nobody suspected his duplicity.
items.meaning: duplicity (n) — dishonest behaviour in which you deceive people by showing one face and hiding another. Adjective: duplicitous.

items.sent: The treatment had terrible side effects, but his remorse was worse: he could not forgive himself for the years he had wasted.
items.meaning: remorse (n) — a deep, painful feeling of being sorry for something wrong you have done. to feel/show remorse; filled with remorse. Adjective: remorseful.

items.sent: She promised herself she would never gamble again, but after six months the temptation was too strong, and she was back at the table.
items.meaning: temptation (n) / to tempt (v) — the wish to do something, especially something you know is wrong or unwise. to resist temptation; to give in to temptation.

items.sent: Nobody could deny the facts, but the accused man remained incredulous to the end, shaking his head as if the evidence described a stranger.
items.meaning: incredulous (adj) — unable or unwilling to believe something. an incredulous look. Compare: incredible = hard to believe (describes the thing, not the person).

vocab.heading: B · Which word means…?
vocab.instruction: Choose from: penitence · potion · relapse. Say the word, then reveal.

items.sent: …a drink with magic, medical or poisonous powers?
items.meaning: a potion (n) — a love potion; a sleeping potion. Mostly in stories, fairy tales and history.

items.sent: …falling back into a bad habit or an illness after a period of improvement?
items.meaning: a relapse (n) / to relapse (v) — He relapsed into his old ways. She had a relapse in March.

items.sent: …being sorry for something wrong you did and wanting to make up for it (a formal, often religious word)?
items.meaning: penitence (n) — tears of penitence. Adjective: penitent. Close to remorse, but penitence usually includes the wish to do better.

vocab.heading: C · Choose the meaning — a / b / c

items.sent:
The documents were sealed and locked away for fifty years, and the historians who wanted to read them had to wait.
  (a) burnt   (b) translated   (c) closed so that nobody could open them without it showing
items.meaning: (c) — to seal (v) — to close an envelope, container or document firmly. Also: a seal (the wax or stamp that closes it); his fate was sealed = it was decided and could not change.

items.sent:
After the scandal the singer went to live abroad, but in his own country he remained a kind of outcast: no one invited him, no one played his songs.
  (a) a person rejected by society   (b) a famous traveller   (c) a criminal in prison
items.meaning: (a) — an outcast (n) — someone who has been driven away or rejected by their group or society. a social outcast.

items.sent:
Her father could not reconcile his love for his son with what the son had done, and the two ideas fought in him until he died.
  (a) forget   (b) make two opposite things fit together   (c) explain to other people
items.meaning: (b) — to reconcile (v) — (1) to find a way for two opposing ideas or facts to exist together; (2) to become friends again after a quarrel. Noun: reconciliation.

vocab_use: Put the ten words in the order they might happen in the life of someone who is leading a double life. Where does it start? Where does it end?
Use duplicity, temptation and remorse to predict what Jekyll will confess.
story_intro: Stevenson's own text, shortened: the two documents Utterson carries home — “Dr Lanyon's Narrative” and “Henry Jekyll's Full Statement of the Case”. Both are written by men who know they are about to die. Read each part; after it, try the quick check from memory, then talk about the question.

check.q: What does Jekyll's letter ask Lanyon to do, and at what time?
check.a: To go to Jekyll's house, have the cabinet forced, take out a particular drawer (powders, a phial and a notebook) and bring it home; then, at midnight, alone, to let in a man who comes in Jekyll's name and give him the drawer.

check.q: What does Lanyon notice about the visitor's clothes, and what does he feel in his presence?
check.a: The clothes are rich and sober but enormously too large for him. Lanyon feels a strange, cold disturbance, a “disgustful curiosity” — and, when the man touches him, “a certain icy pang”.

check.q: What choice does the visitor offer Lanyon — and what does Lanyon choose?
check.a: To let him leave with the glass and stay “neither richer nor wiser”, or to watch and see a prodigy. Lanyon says he has gone too far to stop before he sees the end. He watches Hyde drink and become Henry Jekyll.

story.discuss: Hyde offers Lanyon the choice: stay ignorant or see the truth. Lanyon chooses to see — and it destroys him. Was curiosity his mistake? Would you have looked?

check.q: What was Jekyll's “profound duplicity of life”, and what did he dream of doing about it?
check.a: He hid his undignified pleasures behind a grave, respectable face. He dreamed of separating the two sides of himself into two separate people, so that each could live without the other's shame or restraint.

check.q: Why is Hyde smaller and younger than Jekyll, according to Jekyll?
check.a: Because the evil side of his nature had been less used and less developed than the good — his life had been “nine tenths a life of effort, virtue and control”.

check.q: Why does Jekyll say the drug produced a fiend rather than an angel?
check.a: The drug itself was neither good nor evil; it only released what was in him. He took it out of ambition, not in a noble spirit, so what came out was Edward Hyde.

story.discuss: Looking at Hyde in the mirror, Jekyll feels “no repugnance, rather a leap of welcome. This, too, was myself.” Why is that sentence more frightening than any monster?

check.q: What happened the morning Jekyll woke up and looked at his hand?
check.a: He had gone to bed as Jekyll and woken as Hyde, without taking the drug. It was the first sign that he was losing control of the change.

check.q: Jekyll chose to stay Jekyll. How long did it last, and what does he say about the choice?
check.a: Two months. He says he “chose the better part and was found wanting in the strength to keep to it” — and he never gave up the house in Soho or Hyde's clothes.

check.q: Why can Jekyll not become himself again at the end?
check.a: His original supply of salt has run out, and the new salt doesn't work. He now believes the first supply was impure and that the unknown impurity made the drug work. He is writing under the last of the old powders.

story.discuss: Jekyll's last words are about Hyde: “what is to follow concerns another than myself.” Is he taking responsibility here — or escaping it one last time?

grammar.h2: Grammar — regret: third & mixed conditionals, I wish / If only
grammar.intro: Both documents in this episode are written by men looking back at a choice they cannot undo. The grammar of that is the third conditional (an imagined past), the mixed conditional (an imagined past with a present result) and I wish / If only + past perfect.
notes:
1 · Third conditional — an imagined past with an imagined past result
If + had + past participle,  would / could / might have + past participle
• If the ferry had left on time, we would have caught the train.
• If she hadn't read the small print, she might have signed it.
would have = certain result; might / could have = possible result.

2 · Mixed conditional — an imagined past with a result NOW
If + had + past participle,  would + verb (+ now / today / still)
• If I hadn't lost my passport, I would be in Lisbon now.
• If they had sold the farm in 1990, they would still be rich.
The past is closed; the result is present.

3 · Regret — I wish / If only + past perfect
• I wish I had listened to my grandmother.   (I didn't listen.)
• If only we hadn't bought that car!   (We bought it.)
Careful: I wish I had + past participle is about the past; I wish I had + noun (I wish I had a car) is about now.

exercises.h3: Mixed conditional — a past choice, a present result
exercises.instruction: Complete each sentence. Look carefully: is the gap in the past part or the present part?
items: If Jekyll had never made the drug, he ___ (still / be) a respected doctor today.
If Lanyon hadn't watched the change, he ___ (not / be) dying now.
If Hyde ___ (not / kill) Sir Danvers, he wouldn't be a hunted man now.
Jekyll could become himself again today if the old salt ___ (not / run) out.
If Jekyll ___ (tell) Utterson everything years ago, he wouldn't be so alone now.

exercises.h3: Jekyll's regrets — I wish / If only
exercises.instruction: Write what Jekyll might say. Use the past perfect.
items: I drank the potion that night. → I wish I ___ the potion.
I didn't destroy Hyde's clothes. → If only I ___ Hyde's clothes!
I never told Utterson the truth. → I wish I ___ Utterson the truth.
I kept the house in Soho. → If only I ___ the house in Soho!
I didn't buy more of the first salt. → I wish I ___ more of the first salt.

grammar.outro: Stevenson gives Jekyll no happy “if”. Every conditional in his statement is closed — and that is the tragedy of the grammar as much as of the man.

deeper.h2: Going deeper — looking back at the whole book
paras: Stevenson wrote the first draft in about three days in 1885, in Bournemouth, after a nightmare; his wife woke him because he was crying out, and he was annoyed she had interrupted “a fine bogey tale”. The book sold forty thousand copies in six months and was preached about in churches. It came out in the same decade as the first great arguments about evolution and the mind, when respectable Victorians were beginning to ask what lay underneath the respectable surface.

Look at how the book is built. For eight chapters we are with Utterson, a man who does not want to know, and we see Hyde only from outside, through doors, windows and fog. The explanation comes last, and it comes in documents written by two dead men: nobody in the book is left alive to be asked a question. It is a detective story in which the detective never solves the case — he simply receives the answer in the post.

And look at what the answer is. Hyde is not a monster that got into Jekyll; he is what was already there. Jekyll's real crime is not the drug but the wish behind it: to enjoy his pleasures with none of the consequences, and to stay respected while doing it. That is why “Jekyll and Hyde” has become an everyday English expression — people use it about a charming boss who bullies, or a quiet neighbour with a temper. Everybody knows at least one. Stevenson's worst suggestion is that everybody is at least one.
questions: Jekyll insists, “It was Hyde, after all, and Hyde alone, that was guilty.” By the end, do you believe him? Who killed Sir Danvers Carew?

Utterson, Lanyon, Enfield and Poole all sense that something is wrong, and all of them stay silent for the sake of a gentleman's name. How much of the tragedy is Jekyll's, and how much belongs to the people who protected him?
Jekyll believes the “good” and “evil” in a person could be separated. Is that a comforting idea or a dangerous one? What does modern psychology say about people who divide themselves like this?
Where do you see “Jekyll and Hyde” today — in public life, online, in the workplace? Is the internet the drug that lets people be Hyde with no consequences?

speak.useful: Regret and blame: If he hadn't…, he would never have…; If Lanyon had…, he would still be…; He should have…; I wish he had…; If only…. For a verdict: “Ultimately, the blame lies with…”, “I'd argue that…”, “To be fair to Jekyll…”, “What the ending shows is…”.

tasks.label: Task A · Tell the whole truth (4 minutes)
paras: You are Utterson, and it is midnight. The police are waiting. Tell them what really happened — from the beginning, now that you know: a young doctor with a secret → the dream of separation → the first potion → the mirror → the house in Soho, the will, the cheque → waking as Hyde → the choice → the relapse and the murder → the park bench → the letter to Lanyon → the salt running out → the locked door.

Use at least four conditionals of regret (If he hadn't…, he would…; if only…) and at least five key words (duplicity, remorse, temptation, incredulous, potion, relapse, penitence, seal, outcast, reconcile).

tasks.label: Task B · The trial of Henry Jekyll (4 minutes)
paras: Imagine Jekyll had lived and stood trial for the murder of Sir Danvers Carew. His lawyer argues: the man in the dock did not strike the blow; Hyde did, and Hyde is dead. Be the prosecution or the defence. Give at least three reasons and deal with the other side's strongest point.
Then swap sides for one minute.

tasks.label: Task C · The verdict on the whole book (4 minutes)
paras: Now that you have read it all: was the ending earned? Did Stevenson prepare you for it, or was it a trick? And who, in the end, was to blame for what happened? Give your verdict and defend it.
menu: The ending is perfect: every clue was there from the first chapter, and we simply didn't want to see it.
The mystery works better than the explanation — the book is more frightening before you know the secret.
The real villain of the book is Victorian respectability, not Hyde.
Utterson is the real failure of the story: a good man who always chose silence.
Jekyll deserves some pity: he tried to stop, and a chemical accident decided his fate.
The story is about addiction, and Jekyll behaves exactly like an addict.

final: Jekyll's life is destroyed by something he could do in secret with no one ever knowing. Does being watched make people better? Would you want to live in a world where nobody could hide anything?
“I chose the better part and was found wanting in the strength to keep to it.” Have you ever made a good decision and failed to keep it? What helps people keep a resolution?
If you could recommend this novella to one person you know, who would it be — and what would you tell them before they started?

Before you go — from memory: say one third conditional about Lanyon (If Lanyon had…), one mixed conditional about Jekyll with now or still, and one regret in Jekyll's voice beginning I wish I hadn't…. Then tell me what's wrong with: If Jekyll would have stopped, he would have lived.
